Suspicious bulk orders of used books have raised fresh concerns that AI companies are buying physical books, scanning their contents, and using the text for AI training without paying authors or asking for permission. A new investigation appears to give booksellers their strongest evidence yet after an AirTag hidden inside a rare book ended up at an Amazon AI training facility.

Used-book sellers have reported unusually large orders containing titles with little or no connection to each other. That pattern led some sellers to suspect that buyers were collecting books for large-scale scanning rather than for resale or personal use.

404 Media placed an AirTag inside a shipment of rare books to track where the order went, and the device eventually reached an Amazon facility where workers reportedly scan and destroy books.

Set us as a preferred source and our Apple reporting ranks higher in your Google Search results and Discover feed — one tap, no account changes.

Employees at the facility said large shipments arrive before staff remove the bindings and scan the pages at high speed. The process destroys the original books, which allows workers to handle large volumes of printed material more efficiently.

Why used books matter for AI training

Older books have become especially valuable for AI training because material published before the recent AI boom is less likely to contain text generated or heavily edited by AI systems. That reduces the risk of training newer AI models on content already produced by other AI tools.

The practice has also raised copyright questions because authors generally receive no payment when companies buy second-hand copies and use them for training. US courts have already started addressing whether this type of use qualifies as transformative, while copyright rules in other countries can take a stricter approach.

The AirTag investigation now gives booksellers a clearer picture of where at least some of these unusual bulk orders are going, and it adds more pressure on AI companies to explain how they obtain copyrighted material for training.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: More GTA 6 leaks reveal new details: Cloning keys, combat changes, random bird deaths
articles.subtitle: The latest purported GTA 6 gameplay videos show Jason committing more senseless murder, and reveal even more gameplay systems.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Two legit-looking Grand Theft Auto 6 video clips were posted online yesterday by a person or group going by "Cyberleek," and now the same leaker has posted another two clips and the DMCA takedown notices are flying once again.

The first of the new clips shows a player stealing a cop's motorcycle, driving it into a river, and then casually murdering the inhabitants of an encampment under a freeway. The other clip shows a nighttime raid on an "Allied Crystal" refinery in which the player uses a taser to take out site security before jacking a truck. Like in the other clips, the player is controlling GTA 6's male lead, Jason.

Yesterday, we catalogued 15 interesting details from the first two clips, including a fuel meter and a possible morality system. These new clips have given us more to chew on, and we've collected more notable details from them below.

The leaker responsible for sharing these videos has promised to continue posting clips, so we may well be back with more new details tomorrow. Stay vigilant, though: Alongside these legit-looking (but unconfirmed) leaks, there are also what appear to be AI-generated fakes out there, a problem which will probably only worsen until Rockstar finally hits us with the official reveal, which is scheduled for next Thursday, August 27. The studio has not commented on the source or legitimacy of the leaked videos.

Cloning car keys

When Jason gets close to a car that's not his, there's an option to "Smash Window" (the traditional GTA car-stealing move) or to "Clone Key," which is new. That'd allow players to more quietly steal cars, though it's not shown in the leaked video how it works.

Aim changes

In the clip taken during nighttime, we see Jason steal and use a taser gun. This is our first look at what might be a big change to GTA's combat—the aiming reticle stays on screen at all times while Jason has the gun equipped, ready to fire seemingly without aiming first. Does this mean you can hipfire? Maybe Rockstar wants this GTA to feel genuinely snappy as a cover shooter. If that's the case, maybe sprinting won't require mashing a button anymore.

Greet or taunt?

GTA 5 let you tap a button to make a comment to strangers, but you never really knew what sort of greeting it would be. Something pleasant? Something rude? Probably something rude. The leaked video shows Jason approaching some NPCs under a bridge, and the player can choose to "greet" them or "taunt" them, more in line with the system from RDR2 or Bully. (In the leaked video, the player chooses to stab them to death.)

Looting

Jason loots some bodies during his senseless rampage. You do have to take a moment to reach down toward the body, but it's a much faster animation than in RDR2, where Arthur Morgan would take his sweet time lifting the body and rummaging through pockets. There also appears to be a dedicated item wheel separate from the weapon selection wheel, which would be another RDR2 carryover.

What's up with the dead birds?

Sometimes people wonder, "If cities are full of pigeons, how come we don't see more dead pigeons lying around?" One answer, I've been told, is that the bodies just decompose quite quickly. The other answer is that if you live in an urban area, you do see dead pigeons lying around. I do, at least.

What I have yet to see, however, is a bird drop out of the sky and plop onto the ground in front of me, and then a second bird do the same thing moments later, which happens to Jason as he walks under a freeway in one of the clips. What is going on with the birds?

Zombix

The player uses what appears to be a healing item called "Zombix" and is warned that "repeated use of Zombix will temporarily have a weaker effect on your health."

articles.subtitle: Macworld One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives).
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
One of the things I enjoy doing most with my family is traveling. Annually, we go on two or three domestic trips (at least one of them to Hawaii to visit relatives). We try to go on a big international trip every 18 months or so—I went to South Africa in 2024, and I just got back from a trip to Iceland in August to see the eclipse. And I always take a lot of gear with me.

Every great trip requires planning, whether it’s an overnight stay an hour away from home or a grand vacation in a country I’ve never visited before. Besides all the travel logistics (that my wife handles), there’s the tech you need to bring, which is my responsibility in my household.

Over the years, I’ve figured out what tech I absolutely need to take with me. There’s an art to figuring out what to bring. You don’t want to overdo it, because you’ll end up lugging around stuff you aren’t using. But you don’t want to be left without that thing you absolutely need and don’t really have a means of obtaining that item where you are.

While I now rely on my iPhone for all the photos and videos I shoot, I need other items to ensure a successful and enjoyable trip. Here’s a list of the gear I bring with me on my trips. This is the stuff I almost always bring no matter where I’m going. Hopefully, you can use this list to help you figure out what you need to bring on your next trip. If you have suggestions, drop me a line at rloyola@macworld.com. (Note: Prices stated here are MSRPs, but Amazon often runs sales and discounts on many of them.)

iPhone 17 Pro Max

There was a time when I would bring separate video and still cameras on every trip, but the iPhone has gotten so good, I don’t need any other camera. With some practice and knowledge of iOS’s features and settings, or with third-party camera apps, you can replicate the capabilities of cameras that cost hundreds more. Before the iPhone 17 Pro Max, I used an iPhone 16 Plus, but I really prefer to the Pro’s telephoto lens.

articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

articles.title: Dire Forecast Predicts 39 Million Fewer Consoles Sold If PS6 And Xbox Helix Are $1,000
articles.subtitle: Cheap consoles mean more players. The Wii proved that as competition brought prices down amid the peak of the Xbox 360 and PS3 generations, and the inverse is likely to be true if Sony and Microsoft can’t rein in costs for the PlayStation 6 and Xbox’s...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Cheap consoles mean more players. The Wii proved that as competition brought prices down amid the peak of the Xbox 360 and PS3 generations, and the inverse is likely to be true if Sony and Microsoft can’t rein in costs for the PlayStation 6 and Xbox’s Project Helix. A new report by Ampere Analysis predicts the install base for those next-gen consoles could end up being 38 percent smaller if the hardware is priced at $1,000.

“The economics of console gaming have changed significantly,” Ampere senior research director Piers Harding-Rolls wrote in the August 18 report. “If Sony and Microsoft take conventionally designed, incrementally improved consoles to market at substantially higher prices, our forecasts suggest they risk reducing the addressable audience for the next generation.”

He predicts roughly 39 million fewer PS6s and Project Helix Xboxes will be sold over their first five years if the hardware comes to market priced at $1,000 rather than $700. The forecast also predicts a roughly 12-percent drop in player spending over the first three years of the next console generation if prices skyrocket upward. That’s a difference of about $3.4 billion, much of which would be eaten up by AI-fueled component price hikes rather than going to the people who sell games on the platforms.

The report outlines three possible scenarios to avoid a lost console generation. The first is to delay the launch of the PS6 and Project Helix past their rumored 2028 window until component costs have potentially come back down a bit. The second is to subsidize hardware prices more aggressively. Sony and Microsoft would essentially eat the higher costs to keep the install base growing. The third option is to “substantially innovate” rather than just relying on more power to push graphical fidelity.

It seems hard to see either company taking either of those approaches. Hoping prices magically come back down after 2028 is a huge gamble, and it’s unclear if hardware that’s been in the design phase for years can suddenly be overhauled in favor of a cheaper value proposition that leans on new gimmicks rather than purely boosts to processing power. The good news is that at least both console makers will be facing pressure from the soon-to-be-$500 Switch 2.

Nintendo opted for innovation over power decades ago and it’s now yielded the most affordable console on the market, one that hasn’t had to compromise too much on the quality of its games.

We’re one week away from Grand Theft Auto 6 ’s big Netflix showcase, but the party has already been spoiled. This week, a group called Cyberleek released a cache of leaked GTA 6 gameplay footage — a move meant to punish Rockstar for not releasing a physical disc version of the game, according to Cyberleek’s website. If legitimate, the videos reveal quite a bit about a game that we know next to nothing about, but there’s one thing Cyberleek has yet to spoil: the soundtrack.

More than the wanton violence, music is the lifeblood of the GTA series. It’s what gives each game a distinct sense of identity, with radio stations almost acting as characters. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, for instance, is defined by its west coast hip-hop, grungy 90s alt-rock, and soulful R&B. Grand Theft Auto 5 worked some modern indie rock into the mix, making for an of-the-era blog rock soundtrack featuring bands like Wavves and Ty Segall Band.

So, what kind of sound are we in for with GTA 6? We’ve gotten a few teases already thanks to its official trailers. Tom Petty’s “Love is a Road” and The Pointer Sisters’ “Hot Together” headlined the first two trailers, implying that Rockstar is going for an 80s vibe this time around. That makes perfect sense given the Miami Vice nostalgia of it all.

The leaked footage signals that GTA 6’s soundtrack will still be both genre- and era-spanning, though. The clips only tease a bit of the music that could be featured in GTA 6, with fans identifying one thumping pop song: “ Impact ” by SG Lewis, Robyn, and Channel Tres. Considering that Vice City will likely be filled with nightclubs, it seems pretty reasonable that we’ll get some danceable heaters in there alongside Rockstar’s usual classic rock, hip-hop, and alt-rock selections.

I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: EA employees brace for the worst under Saudi ownership: 'Hard to feel good about being bought out by a regime that's very much at odds with progressive society'
articles.subtitle: Despite assurances from management, some workers believe the company will be subject to censorship by its new owners.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Saudi Arabia's purchase of Electronic Arts, the biggest leveraged buyout in private equity history, officially closed earlier this month. With that deal done, a new Game Developer report has found that an awful lot of employees are expecting much more stringent control over what kinds of games they are and are not allowed to make.

This isn't really new, strictly speaking. After the buyout was announced, current and former EA employees alike expressed concerns about a potential crackdown on some games, particularly those that are visibly diverse and inclusive, like The Sims. Former BioWare lead writer Trick Weekes summed it up aptly, predicting that "guns and football" will be fine, but that "gay stuff" will likely be out.

Despite EA's various efforts to reassure employees that its " cultural values "—a functionally empty term to begin with—will remain intact under Saudi ownership, Game Developer has found that doubts persist among employees. One current employee told the site they believed the purchase was a way to distract from its "regressive" human rights record by "co-opting an established and comparatively progressive company culture."

That's a known phenomenon called "sportswashing," and it's been raised multiple times previously with regards to the EA buyout—in no small part because Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler and, through his chairmanship of the country's Public Investment Fund, EA's new boss, has previously stated outright that he's happy to use it to achieve his goals.

"If sportswashing is going to increase my GDP by way of one percent, then I will continue doing sportwashing," he told Fox News in 2023. "I don't care. "

Being a private company grants EA a certain freedom to do what it likes, but that doesn't mean the company will necessarily just embrace an anti-inclusive agenda: Instead, one employee predicted that "projects just won't get signed because they don't align explicitly with what the Saudi government wants," or that EA won't even pitch them in the first place to avoid antagonizing its new owners.

"It's certainly hard to feel good about being bought out by a regime that's very much at odds with progressive society, so it is surely detrimental to anyone who finds this buyout morally odious," one employee said, raising the point that Saudi Arabia's notoriously oppressive regime is in itself an issue for some employees.

Another said that "if EA had a culture that had any semblance of a moral backbone, it wouldn’t get into bed with a prince who's disgusted by many of its current employees' sexualities and ethnicities," adding that the presence of Jared Kushner, through his Saudi-backed Affinity Partners investment firm, "just adds insult to injury."

The problem many employees are faced with is that moral objections sometimes have to take a back seat to the practicalities of survival, and the videogame industry is in an extremely bad state. One employee said they "feel gross just thinking about it, but there's nowhere else to go. I'd love to leave, but the jobs aren't there, and I have bills to pay.

" Employees who own vested shares in EA will make a good dollar on them thanks to the PIF's premium buyout offer, which may help dull the moral sting, but employees who don't hold shares, including many who are classified as "temporary fulltime," won't even get that.

In a way, that reflects the broader state of EA as a whole.

Being owned by the ruler of a regime that continues to oppress women and members of the LGBTQ+ community, and who is credibly accused of ordering the murder and dismemberment of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018, is bad on its face, but the massive debt EA took on to finance the deal means massive layoffs seem almost inevitable, along with the cancellation of games that don't meet sufficiently lucrative financial targets.

None of that has happened yet, but the mood among the rank and file certainly sounds grim.

"There was a time where execs engaged more and provided more earnest answers about the company, and it genuinely felt like they cared about us," one employee said. "It was years ago though. Now it's mostly just tired corporate bullshit."

articles.title: GTA 6's Newest Gameplay Leak Drama Has Turned Ugly
articles.subtitle: New GTA 6 gameplay clips shared by hacking group mock Rockstar and Take-Two Related Grand Theft Auto 6 has suffered a number of leaks over the years, but none have been quite like the one that transpired this weke.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
New GTA 6 gameplay clips shared by hacking group mock Rockstar and Take-Two

Related

Grand Theft Auto 6 has suffered a number of leaks over the years, but none have been quite like the one that transpired this weke. This time, a hacking activist group called Cyberleek claimed it was sharing unauthorized gameplay clips of Rockstar Games' open-world action game to protest the title's lack of physical discs. A day later, the alleged protest against GTA 6 continued — but so has the fallout.

On Tuesday, Cyberleek shared two short gameplay clips of GTA 6 that depicted previously unseen elements, like melee combat and the return of the six-star Wanted system. Both clips directed viewers to Cyberleek's official website, where the hacking group published a manifesto against Rockstar and GTA 6 publisher Take-Two.

The website spoke out against Take-Two's decision to publish GTA 6 without a physical disc, and expressed worry over the long-term future of digital game distribution. The hackers also voiced displeasure with GTA 6 's $100 Ultimate Edition, which contains exclusive cosmetics and in-game shops. The group concluded its message by threatening to release more clips if Take-Two did not change its release plans.

By Wednesday morning, Cyberleek made good on those threats by publishing a new two-minute GTA 6 gameplay clip. In it, game co-star Jason can be seen tasing a group of people in a restricted area. The clip is watermarked with a tagline that reads, "No physical discs? Then more leeks!" [ sic ]. Later that same day, the hackers published a fourth clip where Jason stabs a police man to death.

As the leaks continue, groups like Stop Killing Games — which advocate for legal protections for digital games when publishers shut off support — have tried distancing themselves from the hacking group. Despite similar overarching aims, a representative from Stop Killing Games reminded GTA 6 fans on social media that the hacking group was doing something illegal. A statement from SKG on Reddit also pointed out that Cyberleek was using its crusade to advertise cryptocurrency and a sketchy meme coin.

Physical game discs were compared to vinyl records

"This kind of act is destructive and helps no one, worse, it risks tarnishing the reputation of our communities and our chances to make change," the statement reads.

Take-Two, for its part, has spent the last day pulling the leaked footage anywhere it has been uploaded. This hasn't stopped people from sharing the content, and in turn, debating its contents. As Kotaku points out, evidence suggests that all the footage shared by Cyberleek is at least a year old, if not older. The final game is likely to resemble much of what has been leaked already, but depending on its age, what ships on Nov. 19 may differ significantly.

This is worth pointing out because, for some, the leaked gameplay footage has proved disappointing. Other fans fear that the footage may signal a graphical downgrade of the game — but that notion isn't helped by the progressive loss of quality with every re-recording and upload. The leaked gameplay also wasn't curated to impress. What Rockstar and Netflix showcase during the streamer's extended look at the open-world game will probably be a better indicator of what GTA 6 will actually be like.

If Cyberleek fears Take-Two's wrath, the hacking group isn't letting on. The last clip shared by the cyber vigilantes mostly shows errant gameplay until the end, when the clip turns into an in-game cutscene with a thinly-veiled barbed message aimed at the publisher.

In it, Jason proposes a toast. "Enjoy your life till the men in suits decide to finally shut you the fuck up," Jason tells Cal Hampton, a GTA 6 supporting character, infamous for his belief in conspiracy theories.

"They don't know nothing about me, man," Hampton responds. "I use a VPN!"

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
The Viking survival exploration game is leaving early access soon

Related

You know what's cool? Vikings. Vikings are cool — unless you are a poor farmer in the kingdom of Northumbria in the early Middle Ages, that is. And if you agree with that statement, you should be happy to know that in just three weeks, everyone will be able to play version 1.0 of Valheim, a Viking-themed exploration and survival game. If you don't agree, then let Odin smite you soon.

Coming from Swedish studio Iron Gate AB, Valheim was released in early access on Steam in 2021. Since then, the game has sold more than 12 million copies, won several accolades, and garnered a rabid fanbase that is waiting with bated breath for the full release. However, I have not played the game yet.

Early access can be a great thing, allowing game developers to grow and fine-tune games in response to player tastes and feedback, but as I discovered Valheim relatively recently, I decided to wait for the full release to experience the game in its full glory on Sept. 9.

Comparing a brutal Viking survival game with Minecraft could seem a stretch at first, but the two titles actually have more in common than it may seem. Valheim takes place in a procedurally generated world inspired by Norse mythology, a purgatory filled with monsters where deceased Vikings have to prove their worth before moving to Valhalla.

Players get to explore mysterious lands and gather resources to build settlements and bases, and to craft and improve their gear. However, rather than letting you swing wildly at pixelated zombies, Valheim offers a challenging dodge-and-block-based combat system, along with area bosses and a plethora of scary enemies. Every area, or biome, has a boss that needs to be defeated before proceeding to the next.

I admit, I have never played Minecraft. The game must be excellent, given its sheer popularity, but I just never saw the appeal in wandering around swinging a pickaxe at rocks to build fancy, Escher-esque architecture. I play games mostly for their story and setting, and while neither of these is the selling point of Mojang Studios' game, Valheim promises to be different.

The rich mythology and folklore of Norse inspiration lend their depth to the game, and the Scandinavian horror vibes that I've seen in trailers and gameplay footage are just my jam. I can endure mining and building a house if, once the work is done, I can go hunting for trolls with my pals. Isn't this what kept the real Vikings going?

Recommended For You

After five years in early access, Valheim has had time to refine and expand. Three major updates have been released during this time, each adding new biomes, bosses, items, and even roleplay elements such as NPCs. At the time of writing, only one biome remains unreleased, which players will finally be able to visit after the game's full launch. Many, including myself, will experience Valheim for the first time on Sept. 9. May Odin guide our spears.

Notch never followed up his miracle creation. Neither did Tetris’ Alexey Pajitnov. How come only one of them could live with it?

articles.title: Review: SuperDuper! 4 gets a stem-to-stern revamp, but is just as seaworthy as ever
articles.subtitle: Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper!…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper! to ensure that all my data is safe and sound. And now, for the first time in a very long time, the venerable backup utility has gotten a top-to-bottom update that brings it into the modern era without sacrificing any of the features—and, most importantly, the reliability—that its users have come to depend on.

While SuperDuper! 4 may look like an entirely new beast, its history has stuck around. It still explains what it’s doing in plain English. It still allows you to make complete, bootable backups. It still has its excellent Smart Update option to optimize the copying process.

But it’s gotten some significant updates too. There’s a new interface, for starters, which conforms to Apple’s current Liquid Glass aesthetic, love it or hate it. It’s a bit of a shock to the system after so long without a change, but it’s hard to deny that the old look had grown somewhat antiquated. The result is an app that makes backups as simple and straightforward as they should be, so that anyone can figure it out: click here to set your destination, choose what method, and click Go.

The changes to SuperDuper! 4 also run more than just skin deep. For example, it’s considerably faster than the previous version—up to an order magnitude faster using the new Turbo implementation of Smart Update, according to Shirt Pocket. That’s borne out in my real-world usage. For example, my last nightly backup of 20.55GB took less than 4 minutes.

There are new capabilities here, too. A new Preview feature lets you perform a dry run of your copy job, letting you see every file that will be changed without actually doing any of it. With a new background helper app, copies won’t interrupt whatever you’re doing. And there’s Shortcuts support, so you can run a workflow when your copy job is completed—or even have one of your shortcuts kick off a copy job.

I’ve been using betas of SuperDuper! 4 for a month or so now, and what’s impressed me most is how much it maintains that set-it-and-forget-it strength of the previous versions. The most important thing for a backup is that element of reliability, so when I open up the app and see “31 successful in a row” note, I know that my data is right where it should be.

And if something goes wrong, it’s easier than ever to see what happened: click on a failed job and you’ll get the details, including an Apple Intelligence-powered summary of the job. (You can get that for completed jobs too. )

There are way more features here too, ones that I just don’t have much reason to use for my purposes, but might just well be what you’re looking for. For example, copy rules that let you handle certain files and folders in granular ways, such as excluding certain ones from backups; support for any file system that macOS understands; and there’s support for multiple copy jobs at the same time, even for those that are scheduled.

Backup apps may not be the most exciting software category, but I dare you to find one that’s more crucial. For me, SuperDuper! has done the job for years and I’ve never had any reason to complain about it. Nothing about that seems poised to change with version 4.

SuperDuper! 4 requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. A free trial version lets you make unlimited full erase backups, but to unlock the rest of the features requires a one-time payment of $43.95. There’s also an upgrade discount for owners of SuperDuper 3 of up to 30 percent. (And, if you bought version 3 very recently, you may be able to get version 4 for free.) And good news: if you need to run backups on older systems, SuperDuper 3 is sticking around.

For everybody who’s already backing up their Macs, SuperDuper! 4 may offer some new features and speed increases that will make the process even smoother. For those of you who aren’t yet…what are you waiting for?

articles.title: I modded GTA 5's NPCs to be punishable for their crimes, and also much more polite
articles.subtitle: Oh, and I still keep falling asleep in the middle of the road.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will, I am assured, have the greatest NPCs of all time. They will be perfect human simulacra, indistinguishable from the meaty lifeforms behind the controller.

My goal: to make GTA 5's barely-living NPCs an approximation of that. So I installed two mods: NPC Check On Player and NPCs Get Wanted Stars. The former makes the citizens of Los Santos more polite—they will get out of their cars and check you are okay if they run you over. The latter makes them punishable when they are impolite—when they commit crimes, they will earn their own wanted stars, and find themselves pursued by cops.

I'll be honest, I mostly installed the NPC Check mod because I hoped it would compel them to stand still when they got wanted stars from hurting me, but hey, it does what it says on the tin. Get pancaked by a car and the driver will screech to a halt, get out, and walk over to check if you're okay.

The problem is that you can only say 'Yes, I'm fine,' which is not really what I want to say to a guy who has just run me over. Plus, the key to say you are fine is Y, which is also the key to go to sleep in my already-installed Roleplay Alone mod. I am constantly getting hit by cars, then falling asleep in the middle of the road as I try to convince the drivers I am okay, which I guess is good enough for them, as they immediately hop back in their rides and drive off.

NPCs Get Wanted Stars, though, is a bit more dramatic. Admittedly, GTA 5's non-playable inhabitants aren't exactly prone to random criminal acts, so you do have to bait them into it.

My advice? Run into them at a full sprint over and over again, until they (unreasonably) get mad enough to throw a punch at you. Ideally, do this in front of a police station, then sit back and smirk as the 5-0 chase down their perp, cuff them, and stand around rather confused about what, exactly, to do next, as if they've not been trained for outcomes that don't involve a bullet-riddled suspect.

The realism is off the charts.

Mosaic is a baseball app that’s been in TestFlight for a few months. (Scroll back through Weingardt’s Threads history for details. ) From the moment I saw it, I was dazzled—it’s a great iOS baseball app that uses all of Apple’s platform technologies to lay out live game data and show off other MLB features in ways that MLB’s own app just doesn’t.

And it even integrated with MLB TV, so if you’re a subscriber to MLB’s premium video service, you can watch games via Mosaic, including in the most mind-blowing multiview I’ve seen.

I don’t want to lean too much into the current state of the official MLB app, but it used to be so cutting-edge and great that when I was at Macworld, we gave it a zillion awards and ended up just inducting it into our “app hall of fame.” But over the years, that app has become generic and unfocused and one-size-fits-all. Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: No More PlayStation Discs Means No More Disc Butts
articles.subtitle: Bloodborne Far Cry Overwatch Uncharted 4 Sony is ending its physical disc production for PlayStation games beginning in 2028.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Bloodborne Far Cry Overwatch Uncharted 4

Sony is ending its physical disc production for PlayStation games beginning in 2028. A lot of people are very reasonably worried about this for very valid reasons: there are concerns around digital ownership, the decimation of the used games market, worries this may price some people out of buying games entirely, or just frustration around not being able to hold a disc in one’s hand. I want to be clear that I think these concerns are all important and valid, and I think this is a terrible move on Sony’s part.

But today I also want to whine about a trivial knock-on effect that I keep thinking about: Sony getting rid of discs means no more new Disc Butts.

What’s a Disc Butt? I’m so glad you asked. A Disc Butt is when the image on a video game disc lines up perfectly in such a way where you can put two fingers together up against the back of the disc and make it look like the character on the front of the disc has a naked butt. The most famous example of this is Bloodborne, of course, as shown here:

But Overwatch did something similar:

HAHAHAHAHAHAHA BUTTS #Blizzard #Overwatch #Tracer pic.twitter.com/lCKoKJ4sOI — Stacey Jenkins 💀⚰️ (@HereLiesStacey) May 25, 2016

HAHAHAHAHAHAHA BUTTS #Blizzard #Overwatch #Tracer pic.twitter.com/lCKoKJ4sOI

— Stacey Jenkins 💀⚰️ (@HereLiesStacey) May 25, 2016

And other games like Far Cry: Primal and Uncharted 4 have offered, uh, alternative opportunities for goofing around with fingers and discs.

If you already own these discs, your ability to make fun little butts and things with those existing discs isn’t going away. But we’re never going to have any new ones after 2028 for PlayStation games, and conceivably not for Xbox games, either, if the rumors are true.

“But Reb,” you say, “surely companies have learned their lesson and would never produce a disc that allowed for a Disc Butt again anyway?” Absolutely not. Companies never learn lessons. I am certain that were discs allowed to continue, someone would once again put a character in a, um, compromising position on a disc, and we’d get to do this gag again and again. But after 2028, it’s as good as over. No matter how much we yell at Sony about it.

I know this isn’t anywhere near the biggest issue with the end of physical games. I’m personally pretty pissed off about how this means I’ll never be able to truly own any of my new PlayStation games after 2027, and I’ve written before about how much I already miss video game bargain bins.

But it sucks to lose the ability to hold a thing in your hands and manipulate it and draw on it and share it with a friend and have your younger sibling scratch the hell out of it and otherwise mess it up. You could argue some of those things are inconveniences we’re best rid of, and I feel like I’m turning into an old fogey (in my 30s) being upset about it, but I just liked it when stuff was real, you know?

Also, butts are funny! I’m sad there will be no new little Disc Butts to be made. Bloodborne will just have to keep me company forever.

articles.title: TerminalWidget makes custom widget building easy
articles.subtitle: A TerminalWidget shortcut action and its output. I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a glance. My tool of choice for this is SwiftBar, itself a follow-on to BitBar (which has been rebooted as xbar ). On my iPad, I’ve been using custom widgets generated with Simon Støvring’s Scriptable app to do the job.

Now here’s a new contender that generates widgets on both Mac and iOS: Brett Terpstra’s $20 TerminalWidget, which lets you send data to a widget from a command-line script, Shortcut, AppleScript, or a URL scheme.

Widgets are more complicated than little items that live in the menu bar. That’s why Scriptable uses little JavaScript scripts to build them. TerminalWidget has a basic set of terminology that lets you target specific widgets and provides some pre-filled functionality that lets you generate some design elements without much hassle. It’ll also just… take text you give it and display it if you want.

If you’re working via Shortcuts, you can update TerminalWidget using a bunch of different template types: Chart, Image, Progress, Table, or Text. Just as with the command line, each Shortcuts action contains a bunch of variables, so you can customize colors and fonts, add a caption and title, or other things that help fill out TerminalWidget’s templates.

It’s by design a lot less flexible than something like Scriptable, where the sky’s the limit—but it’s also a lot more approachable, since you’re basically filling in the blanks with whatever data you want to provide.

I wasn’t really able to replicate my beloved Scriptable weather widget in TerminalWidget—not flexible enough—but TerminalWidget also supports straight-up image use, which allowed me to generate the contents of my Scriptable widget via script, output it as an image, and then tell TerminalWidget to load that image. So if you wanted to offload widget duties to your Mac or a remote server, you could do that and just display the image in TerminalWidget.

In a way, TerminalWidget turns its limitation (lack of flexibility) into a strength, because the learning curve is so gentle, especially if you use Shortcuts, which literally shows you every single possible variable you could possibly use, so you can tinker and figure out what you want to display. Dr. Drang is using it for planetary positions, because that tickles his fancy.

If there’s something you’d like to put on a glanceable widget across iPad, iPhone, and Mac, TerminalWidget will let you do it. That’s a beautiful thing. Now I need to figure out what widgets to add to my own devices…

articles.title: OpenAI explains what will happen when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend
articles.subtitle: It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.title: Jason Statham's Mutiny Debuts With Horrible Rotten Tomatoes Score
articles.subtitle: Mutiny is no Beekeeper Related Jason Statham, the master of the mid action movie, has a new film out this week. While Mutiny won't be released in theaters until Friday, critic reviews are out now, and they paint a disappointing picture of Statham's latest.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Mutiny is no Beekeeper

Related

Jason Statham, the master of the mid action movie, has a new film out this week. While Mutiny won't be released in theaters until Friday, critic reviews are out now, and they paint a disappointing picture of Statham's latest.

Mutiny is directed by Jean-François Richet, the visionary behind 2023's Gerard Butler and Mike Colter vehicle Plane. It stars Statham as a guy with vaguely ex-cop or special forces experience on board a human trafficking boat trying to transport women and children. Statham — you'll never guess — beats the evil guys up. That's basically all there is to it.

The movie is a cool 95 minutes, meaning there isn't much need for anything but action sequences. Mutiny is another entry in the Statham action portfolio, joining the likes of The Transporter, The Mechanic, The Beekeeper, A Working Man, and Shelter.

While Statham's action flicks have a charm all their own, and have earned some praise from critics in the past, Mutiny is not having similar luck. Rotten Tomatoes currently has the film sitting at 41% with 22 reviews. That's certified rotten.

Most critics aren't holding back their disdain for Mutiny, with one review saying the film "has so little personality that you could place it in a bus station, and the experience wouldn't change one bit. Nobody involved seems to care, and neither should we. " Matt Goldberg at Commentary Track chimed in, saying that Mutiny "feels like a waste" of Statham's talents.

There's a difference between good schlock and bad schlock, with Statham often delivering the former. It's too bad Mutiny seems to be the latter.

There are, however, some defenders of Mutiny. Owen Gleiberman writes in Variety that "It’s all in the timing — the rhythm of revenge murder that’s perfect, because it’s done by any means necessary. Jason Statham is keeping that dream alive.

" Ian Sandwell at Digital Spy gets to the heart of Mutiny, saying that "It won't convert anybody who foolishly isn't a fan of 'Jason Statham gets revenge', but everybody else will have a damn good time. " That is a sentiment that probably clears up for readers whether they'll enjoy Mutiny or not. It's Statham killing guys on a boat; you know if you like it already.

Mutiny lands in theaters on Aug. 21.

articles.title: App report: Talk back and track on a Mac
articles.subtitle: Clearly, creating Mac apps that make the most of your voice continues to be a focus of developers — at least based on the offerings coming across my radar lately.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Clearly, creating Mac apps that make the most of your voice continues to be a focus of developers — at least based on the offerings coming across my radar lately. Following last week’s profile of two different takes on on-device transcription software, we’ve got yet another voice-powered app to take a look at, with this macOS download supporting dictation that you can then paste into other apps.

But other apps are finding different ways to make some noise, including a pair of simple-yet-satisfying utilities and an old favorite that’s learned some new tricks. If you’ve got an app that you’d like to bring to our attention, let us hear about it at apps@sixcolors.com, adding a brief description on what the app does and what devices it supports.

And now, on to the business at hand. Or at voice, as the case may be.

Lesskeys

Some times, it’s better to dictate than to type, and Lesskeys looks to make that process as simple as possible. With the app running in your menu bar, just hit a hotkey — it’s Option-Period by default — to start recording your dulcet tones. As you speak, your words are captured in a clipboard that you can copy and paste into any app once you stop recording by tapping the hotkey again.

Alternatively, you can also hold down the hotkey to jot down quick thoughts with the recording stopping once you release the keys.

Lesskeys’ bag of tricks extends beyond just dictation. There’s a command for recording phone calls made through your Mac, and you can also import audio and video files to be transcribed. Additionally, the app boasts the ability to identify speakers when you record conversations. Power users will also appreciate how Lesskeys lets you set up different configurations for different apps, such as a different language, model or prompt when a particular app is in the foreground.

Lesskeys is free to download, but you’re limited to 5 minutes of dictation per day, along with five audio and video transcriptions each. That should be enough of a ceiling to test out the app and decided whether it’s worth the one-time $49.99 Pro license to remove any restrictions.

PeekNote

If you’re like me, you put the Mac’s clipboard through quite a workout, copy and pasting various text snippets, URLs and other captured material into different apps. And if you’re even more like me, you wind up using a lot of the same snippets and URLs over and over again. PeekNote is a handy macOS utility that keeps frequently used snippets close at hand.

Essentially, PeekNote is a floating window where you can stack multiple bits of text to paste into any window on your desktop. As I’m applying for a lot of jobs at the moment, I can use the PeekNote window to stash links to articles and other parts of my profile that I frequently use in cover letters and web forms.

Pay a one-time $9.99 fee, and you unlock the full app, which includes the ability to create 22 different tabs for organizing related text blocks. The unlocked version of PeekNote also lifts any limitations on the number of blocks.

If I had a suggestion for PeekNote, it would be to make it easier to shrink the app window so that it only expands when you need access to one of the text blocks you’ve got stored in there. But otherwise, it’s a fine utility when you want frequently used links and snippets to be right at your fingertips.

Carrot Weather

If you’ve looked beyond the built-in Weather app on your iPhone, you doubtlessly have some familiarity with Carrot Weather and its… unique take on delivering the forecast. The app, which works across a host of Apple devices including the Mac, Apple Watch and Vision Pro, tells you the weather with attitude, using a sliding snark scale that you can adjust to your liking.

Additionally, as you can see from this 2023 Six Colors profile, developer Grailr has built some other high-end capabilities and customization features into the app, the more intriguing of which are positioned behind a paywall.

Carrot Weather is worth revisiting these days thanks to an added feature that arrived over the summer — a trip planner capability for the iPhone version that lets you track the forecast for any upcoming getaways. I’ve got a trip to Detroit in my immediate future, and when I head over to the Locations section of Carrot Weather, I can see that I had better pack an umbrella for the thunderstorm that’s forecast on at least one day of my trip.

The 6.7 update to Carrot Weather also introduced new custom notifications that alert you when a data point hits a certain threshold — say, a temperature drop or a rise in UV index levels. Both the Trip Planner and custom notification features require a Premium Ultra subscription that costs $9.99/month.

Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

Pastebot 3’s main menu.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. Not only does the update add MCP support, making it an excellent tool to use with Claude or ChatGPT/Codex, but it includes a brand new CLI that you or an agent can use from Terminal or incorporate into scripts you build. Commands include:

Browse and search clipboard history

Filter results by Pastebin or date

Retrieve the full text of a clipping

Retrieve images from clippings

List available Pastebot filters

Apply filters to clippings or supplied text

Place an existing clipping on the clipboard

Create new text or image clippings

Paste clipboard contents into the frontmost app

Delete individual clippings
